results.title: BOJ holds rate at 1% as expected, one board member backs 0.25% hike
results.brief_text: The Bank of Japan voted 8 to 1 to keep its policy interest rate at 1% at today's meeting. Board member Hajime Takata was the sole dissenter, proposing a hike to 1.25%, and warned that underlying inflation could accelerate above the 2% target in the second half of fiscal 2026, driven by wage increases, crude oil prices, and a weak yen. The decision to hold rates came after reports that Japan intervened in the yen market yesterday, causing the yen to strengthen sharply from 163 yen per US dollar to 157.96 yen per dollar. Analysts are watching Governor Kazuo Ueda's press conference for signals on the future direction of monetary policy.

results.title: BOJ Expected to Hold Policy Rate Steady at July Meeting, Maintain Vigilance on Upside Price Risks
results.brief_text: The Bank of Japan is expected to keep its policy rate unchanged at 1 percent at its monetary policy meeting on July 30 and 31. At the previous meeting in June, the BOJ raised rates for the first time in six months, and it will now assess the impact of that decision. In its Outlook Report to be released at the same time, the BOJ is likely to reiterate its vigilance against upside risks to prices, as the underlying inflation rate approaches the 2 percent target, and signal its intention to continue raising rates going forward. While the economic outlook is expected to be revised up slightly, the price outlook is seen largely unchanged from the previous report in April. The BOJ views that downside risks to the economy have receded due to progress in alternative procurement of critical supplies amid heightened tensions in the Middle East, and that stronger AI-related demand is providing support. On upside price risks, the tail risk of crude oil supply disruptions that was flagged in April has diminished, but upward pressure from alternative procurement costs, AI-related demand, and yen depreciation is expected to be emphasized. With underlying inflation nearing 2 percent, Deputy Governor Shinichi Uchida has said that it is necessary to be mindful of upside risks, and the Outlook Report is expected to maintain vigilance while noting the need to confirm that underlying inflation is firmly anchored in order to achieve the price target. Regarding the dollar-yen exchange rate, which rose above 163 yen for the first time in 40 years, some within the BOJ say the yen's weakness is already within expectations and does not mean upside price risks are rapidly increasing, while others note that financial conditions remain accommodative and, depending on risks, call for rate hikes at intervals shorter than once every six months.

results.title: Bank of Japan to Decide on First Rate Hike in Three Months Amid Inflation Concerns
results.brief_text: The Bank of Japan is considering a rate hike at its monetary policy meeting on September 17 and 18, which would be its first in three months. The corporate goods price index rose 7.2 percent in July from a year earlier, reflecting persistent upward price pressure from AI-related demand and the weak yen. At the July meeting, some board members called for a faster pace of rate increases, and a hike at this meeting would signal an acceleration of the future tightening path. Long-term interest rates climbed to 2.9 percent in July, the highest in about 30 years, and the impact of faster rate hikes on market rate expectations will be a key focus.

results.title: BOJ signals further rate hikes, warns weak yen risks stoking inflation
results.brief_text: The Bank of Japan signalled it may raise interest rates again after holding its policy rate steady at 1 percent at today's meeting, saying inflation risks rising due to the weak yen, elevated crude oil prices, and businesses passing on wage costs to selling prices. The BOJ also warned that the yen's depreciation, trading near its lowest level in over 39 years against the US dollar, is likely to push up prices especially for durable goods, and that artificial intelligence-related demand could also cause inflation to rebound. In its quarterly economic outlook report, the BOJ expects the consumer price index to accelerate clearly above 2 percent from the second half of fiscal 2026, while raising its growth forecast for Japan's economy to 0.6 percent in fiscal 2026 and 0.8 percent in fiscal 2027. It lowered its core CPI forecast for fiscal 2026 to 2.5 percent and raised it for fiscal 2027 to 2.4 percent.

results.title: BOJ signals possible faster rate hike on heightened inflation risk concerns
results.brief_text: The Bank of Japan released a summary of opinions from its July policy meeting, noting that board members see growing risks that could push inflation higher. One of the nine members said core consumer inflation is approaching two percent and that greater attention should be paid to upside inflation risks than before, suggesting the timing of a policy rate hike could come sooner than markets expect. At the meeting on July thirtieth and thirty-first, the board voted to keep the policy rate at one percent and signaled a possible rate increase in September, while monitoring the impact of the weak yen on prices and economic growth. The summary also showed another member said that although the neutral rate cannot be pinpointed precisely, the BOJ needs to raise the policy rate, which remains below the lower bound of a broadly estimated range of one point one to two point five percent, to lay the groundwork for normalizing monetary policy. In addition, the BOJ projects core consumer inflation will rise two point five percent in fiscal twenty twenty-five and two point four percent in fiscal twenty twenty-six, while revising up its economic growth forecast to zero point eight percent from zero point seven percent.

results.title: BOJ minutes show board members support further rate hikes to control long-term yields
results.brief_text: Minutes from the Bank of Japan's June meeting show that some board members backed additional rate increases to stabilise long-term interest rates that have surged on inflation concerns. At the meeting on 15 and 16 June, the board raised the policy rate from 0.75 percent to 1 percent, the highest level in 31 years. Several members called for continued rate hikes, citing a weak yen, higher import costs, and the pass-through of costs to private-sector selling prices. Meanwhile, long-term Japanese government bond yields hit a 29-year high amid fiscal worries and inflation fears from the war in Iran that has pushed up oil prices. A minority of members viewed the spike in long-term rates as driven mainly by Middle East factors, and noted that raising the policy rate to maintain price stability would lead to stability in long-term rates, reflecting the BOJ's intention to respond to the surge in long-term yields.

results.title: Bank of Japan raises interest rates to 1%, highest since 1995
results.brief_text: The Bank of Japan raised its short-term policy rate from 0.75% to 1%, a level last seen in 1995, as it moves to normalize monetary policy amid mounting inflation pressures. The decision was approved in a 7-1 vote, with board member Toichiro Asada dissenting due to concerns that the Middle East conflict poses a bigger threat to economic growth than inflation. The central bank also said it will continue cutting government bond purchases by 200 billion yen each quarter, eventually reducing monthly purchases to 2 trillion yen from April 2027. The yen carry trade is gaining momentum again, with leveraged funds boosting their bets against the yen to more than 115,000 contracts in the week ended June 9, the largest bearish position since November 2017, according to CFTC data. At the time of writing, the yen was trading at 160.29 per dollar, while yields on 10-year Japanese government bonds rose 3 basis points to 2.647%.

results.title: Market prices in 82% chance of BOJ rate hike in September
results.brief_text: The market has raised the probability that the Bank of Japan will raise interest rates at its September 18 meeting to 82%, up from just 23% before the July meeting. Senior BOJ officials are scheduled to deliver several speeches before the meeting, which will be watched for signals supporting or opposing this rate hike. Deputy Governor Ryozo Himino is due to speak this Thursday, while Governor Kazuo Ueda may comment after the G20 meeting in the United States next week. BOJ board members Hajime Takata and Kazuyuki Masu will speak on September 2 and September 10 respectively. Kento Minami, senior economist at Daiwa Securities, believes the BOJ may not explicitly say it will raise rates, but will emphasize upside inflation risks, which the market will interpret as opening the door for a rate hike next month. A key support comes from the United States and Japan jointly intervening in currency markets in late July for the first time since 1998, helping pull the yen back from levels near 160 yen per dollar. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said monetary policy needs to follow through on the currency intervention measures, and expressed confidence that the BOJ will take necessary action.

raw_responses.title: Hitachi Q1 FY2027 adjusted operating profit up 39.5%, full-year forecast raised
raw_responses.brief_text: Hitachi announced its first-quarter results for the fiscal year ending March 2027, with adjusted operating profit, which reflects the strength of its core business, rising 39.5% year-on-year to 294.3 billion yen. Revenue increased 20.0% to 2.7096 trillion yen, and the adjusted operating profit margin improved from 9.3% to 10.9%. The energy business led the company, with segment profit surging 64.5% to 129.0 billion yen, driven by global power demand and data center investments centered on the power grid. All four reported segments achieved higher revenue and profit. The company raised its full-year earnings forecast and interim dividend outlook. Meanwhile, quarterly profit attributable to owners of the parent edged down 1.4% to 189.4 billion yen due to a decline in financial income.

raw_responses.title: Auto plant shutdowns prolonged after Kumamoto earthquake, Toyota and Nissan extend production halts
raw_responses.brief_text: The shutdown of auto plants is dragging on following the Kumamoto earthquake. Toyota Motor, Nissan Motor, and Daihatsu Motor have extended the suspension of plant operations and production of some models from the 5th to the 7th of this month due to parts supply disruptions. The impact has spread to plants on Honshu, with no timeline given for resumption. Meanwhile, semiconductor plants concentrated in Kyushu are making progress in recovery. raw_responses.title: iPhone 18 Rumors Point to Smaller Dynamic Island, 12GB RAM, and 2-Nanometer A20 Chip
raw_responses.brief_text: The latest iPhone 18 rumors reveal key details including a potentially smaller Dynamic Island on Pro models, a RAM upgrade to 12GB on standard models, and a 2-nanometer A20 chip that may come with a significantly higher cost. Reports indicate the standard iPhone 18 will be delayed to early 2027, separating it from the Pro models which are still expected to launch in September 2026. In terms of design, the standard model is expected to retain a look similar to the iPhone 17, but may adopt a smaller Dynamic Island like the Pro models, while the Camera Control button could be removed to cut costs. As for the A20 chip manufactured on TSMC's 2-nanometer process, analyst Jeff Pu says it will be about 15 percent faster and use about 30 percent less power compared to the A19, but the cost per chip could reach 280 dollars, an increase of about 80 percent from the previous generation. Combined with TSMC raising production prices by about 10 percent in July 2026, many expect Apple to increase the price of the iPhone 18. On the RAM front, the standard iPhone 18 is reported to get 12GB of LPDDR5X RAM, up from 8GB in the iPhone 17, but well-known analyst Ming-Chi Kuo disagrees, stating that Apple may opt for 9GB of RAM instead of 12GB. Camera system specifications remain unclear, but reports suggest Apple may continue using Sony sensors, despite earlier rumors that Samsung could become a sensor supplier.

raw_responses.brief_text: Nvidia and Kawasaki Heavy Industries have agreed to co-develop AI-powered robotics for shipbuilding in Japan. raw_responses.title: Casio Launches the Casio Mini Home Calculator, a Low-Price Explosive Hit
raw_responses.brief_text: On August 2, 1972, Casio Computer launched the Casio Mini home calculator. It was a product that miniaturized and lowered the price of calculators, which had been mainly for business use, making them suitable for home use, priced at 12,800 yen. This was achieved by reducing costs in the LSI and key components. With a six-digit display and only addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division functions, it became a massive hit, selling one million units in less than a year after release. This development philosophy of small and cheap became established as a winning pattern for Japanese manufacturing as a whole.

raw_responses.title: Morgan Stanley lifts Amazon price target but overlooks AI investment risks
raw_responses.brief_text: Amazon stock closed the July 31 trading session up 15.32% at $271.58, soaring after its second quarter 2026 earnings report. Morgan Stanley analyst Brian Nowak raised the price target to $335 from $330, maintaining an overweight rating, citing AWS growth acceleration to 36.8% year over year and a $496 billion backlog that beat expectations by about $20 billion. However, the bullish thesis ignores that AWS growth is largely driven by unprofitable AI startups Anthropic and OpenAI, both heavily funded by Amazon, and that Amazon’s Q2 net income of $62.6 billion included a $53.4 billion non-operating gain from its Anthropic investment. The analysis also overlooks the potential entry of Meta into the cloud infrastructure market, which could spark a price war, and the difficulty of monetizing private AI valuations, as evidenced by SoftBank’s stalled efforts to secure a loan using OpenAI shares as collateral.

aspects.reason: Morgan Stanley raises price target to $335, citing AWS growth and backlog, but ignores AI investment risks.

raw_responses.title: AI Drives Up US Cost of Living, from Electricity Bills to Electronics
raw_responses.brief_text: Artificial intelligence, developed to boost efficiency, is becoming a pressure pushing up the cost of living in the United States, with households spending an average of over 375 dollars more per year due to surging energy, chip, and construction material costs driven by the AI investment wave, which is expected to reach around 750 billion dollars in 2026. Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, estimates that this impact has added about 0.2 percentage points to inflation. Household electricity prices in 2025 rose twice as fast as normal and were still about 4 percent higher than the previous year during the first five months of 2026, while wholesale prices for semiconductors and electronic components in June surged 26 percent from a year earlier. This led Apple to raise prices on some models by about 20 percent, Microsoft to increase Xbox prices by roughly 25 percent, and Sony to hike PlayStation prices. Microsoft also raised Microsoft 365 subscription prices by as much as 43 percent after adding the AI Copilot feature. Furthermore, the rush to build data centers is driving up demand for copper and construction labor, with construction wages growing faster than the average, which could worsen housing affordability in the future.

aspects.reason: Microsoft increased Xbox prices by ~25% and Microsoft 365 subscription prices by up to 43% after adding AI Copilot.

Furthermore, the rush to build data centers is driving up demand for copper and construction labor, with construction wages growing faster than the average, which could worsen housing affordability in the future.
